sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    REQ[request] --> MW1[mw1: logging] --> MW2[mw2: auth] --> H[handler]
    MW2 -->|401 reject| R[return without next]
    H --> RES[response]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The execution order, precisely: middleware[0] wraps middleware[1] wraps ... wraps the handler. Request flows OUT-IN (0→1→...→handler), response flows IN-OUT. The wrap-in-reverse in a chain function exists because each mw takes the NEXT thing to call — building from the innermost outward means iterating the slice backward.

The pre/post asymmetry: BEFORE next(), you own the request — modify it (add context values, change r), write headers (w.Header().Set before any Write), even short-circuit (return without calling next — auth reject, rate-limit). AFTER next(), the response is committed — you can't change headers/status (already sent); you CAN observe (log duration, count status from a recording wrapper) and clean up.

The short-circuit pattern, which is middleware's most important behavior: auth middleware checks the token; invalid → WriteHeader(401) and RETURN (no next call). The handler never runs. This is how middleware does enforcement — the wrapping makes it apply to every handler in the chain, consistently.

The panic-recovery middleware — the one every service needs: the deferred func inside the wrapper catches the panic, writes a 500, logs the stack — the goroutine-per-request model means an unhandled panic would crash the whole server without the middleware boundary (net/http actually recerves handler panics per-connection since 1.6, but a middleware recovery gives you logging and clean 500s).
